questions.q: A 28-year-old farmer presents with 3 well-defined hypopigmented patches with partial loss of sensation and slightly enlarged ulnar nerve. Slit skin smear is negative. Biopsy shows epithelioid cell granulomas with lymphocyte cuffing. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.exp: Borderline tuberculoid (BT) leprosy with <5 patches and negative slit skin smear is classified as paucibacillary. WHO MDT-PB regimen: Rifampicin 600mg monthly supervised + Dapsone 100mg daily for 6 months.

questions.q: A 22-year-old college student presents with hypopigmented, finely scaly macules over the chest and upper back. KOH mount of scale shows short curved hyphae and clusters of spores resembling 'spaghetti and meatballs'. Which topical agent is the first-line treatment?
questions.exp: Pityriasis versicolor is caused by Malassezia furfur. KOH shows short hyphae and round spores ('spaghetti and meatballs'). Selenium sulfide 2.5%, zinc pyrithione shampoo, or ketoconazole shampoo applied and left on are first-line topical treatments.

questions.q: A 5-year-old child presents with multiple honey-crusted vesicles and pustules clustered around the mouth and nose. Satellite lesions are spreading to cheeks. The most common causative organism of this type of superficial bacterial skin infection is:
questions.exp: Staphylococcus aureus is now the predominant organism in non-bullous impetigo. Bullous impetigo is exclusively staphylococcal (phage type 71, exfoliative toxin A/B). Streptococcus pyogenes can cause non-bullous impetigo but is less common. Topical mupirocin is first-line for localized disease.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with painful oral erosions for 3 months, followed by flaccid blisters over the trunk that rupture easily leaving raw erosions. Nikolsky's sign is positive. Histopathology shows suprabasal acantholysis with 'tombstone' arrangement of basal cells. The primary target antigen is:
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris targets Desmoglein 3 (found predominantly in mucous membranes) causing oral lesions, and Desmoglein 3 + 1 when skin is involved. Desmoglein 1 alone is the target in pemphigus foliaceus (superficial, no oral lesions). IIF on monkey esophagus shows intercellular IgG deposits.

questions.q: A 30-year-old man presents with a single, deep, painful genital ulcer with undermined, ragged edges and a necrotic base. Ipsilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy (bubo) is present. Gram stain of ulcer discharge shows small gram-negative coccobacilli in a 'school of fish' pattern. The most likely diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Chancroid caused by Haemophilus ducreyi presents with painful, soft, non-indurated ulcer with undermined edges. 'School of fish' or 'railroad track' pattern on Gram stain. Bubo (fluctuant inguinal lymph node) in 50%. Syphilitic chancre is painless and indurated. Treatment: azithromycin 1g single dose or ceftriaxone 250mg IM.

questions.q: A 32-year-old HIV-positive patient (CD4 count 90 cells/μL) presents with numerous large (>5 mm) pearly, umbilicated papules distributed over the face, neck, and trunk. Some lesions are confluent. The most important treatment approach to control this condition is:
opts: Topical imiquimod 5% cream applied to all lesions
Systemic cryotherapy to all lesions weekly
Antiretroviral therapy (ART) to restore immune function
questions.exp: In severely immunocompromised HIV patients, molluscum contagiosum (Poxvirus) causes extensive, large, atypical lesions. Restoration of immune function via ART is the cornerstone — lesions resolve with immune reconstitution. Local destructive therapy (cryotherapy, curettage) provides temporary relief but lesions recur without immune recovery.

questions.q: A 40-year-old woman presents with 3-month history of proximal muscle weakness, dysphagia, and heliotrope rash around the eyes. On examination, flat-topped, violaceous papules are noted over the dorsal MCP and PIP joints bilaterally. Which term describes this pathognomonic sign?
questions.exp: Gottron's papules are flat-topped violaceous papules over the dorsal knuckles (MCP, PIP joints) — pathognomonic of dermatomyositis. Mechanic's hands (cracked, hyperkeratotic lateral fingers) are associated with antisynthetase syndrome. Both heliotrope rash and Gottron's papules together are considered definitive for dermatomyositis.

questions.q: A 65-year-old farmer presents with a slow-growing, pearly, translucent nodule with rolled edges and surface telangiectases over the nasolabial fold. Central ulceration is noted. This is the most common skin cancer. What is the single most important aetiological factor?
questions.exp: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is the most common skin cancer, with cumulative UV radiation (especially UVB) as the primary risk factor. Classic nodular BCC: pearly nodule with rolled edges, telangiectases, and central ulceration ('rodent ulcer'). BCC rarely metastasizes (<0.1%) but causes significant local tissue destruction.

questions.q: A 22-year-old patient started on dapsone for leprosy develops acute jaundice, pallor, and dark urine within 4 weeks. Peripheral blood smear shows fragmented red cells and 'bite cells'. Which enzyme deficiency markedly increases the risk of this adverse effect?
questions.exp: Dapsone causes dose-dependent methemoglobinemia and hemolytic anemia in all patients, but G6PD deficiency dramatically amplifies hemolysis. G6PD screening before starting dapsone is recommended, especially in populations with high prevalence (South Asian, African). Bite cells result from Heinz body removal by splenic macrophages.

questions.q: A leprosy patient on multidrug therapy suddenly develops redness, swelling, and pain in his existing skin patches, with new erythematous patches appearing. He has no fever, no new nodules, and no systemic symptoms. Which type of leprosy reaction is this, and what is the immediate management?
questions.exp: Type 1 (reversal) reaction occurs in borderline leprosy (BT, BB, BL) due to sudden increase in cell-mediated immunity. Presents with inflamed, edematous existing lesions, new lesions, and nerve involvement. Systemic corticosteroids (prednisolone 40-60 mg/day, tapering over 6 months) are the mainstay. MDT must be continued.

questions.q: A 35-year-old man with widespread psoriasis has PASI score 18, BSA 22%, and DLQI 15. He has failed methotrexate and cyclosporine. According to standard criteria for initiating biologic therapy in psoriasis, which statement is correct?
opts: PASI ≥10 AND DLQI ≥10 after failure of 2 conventional agents qualifies for biologics
Biologics are indicated only if BSA >30%
questions.exp: Biologics (TNF-alpha inhibitors, IL-17, IL-23 inhibitors) are indicated for moderate-severe psoriasis: PASI ≥10 AND DLQI ≥10, after inadequate response to at least 2 conventional systemic agents (methotrexate, cyclosporine, acitretin). This patient qualifies (PASI 18, DLQI 15) with failure of 2 prior agents.

questions.q: A 45-year-old diabetic man presents with reddish-brown, well-demarcated, velvety patches in the bilateral axillae and groin. KOH mount is negative. Wood's lamp shows bright coral-red fluorescence. The causative organism is:
questions.exp: Erythrasma is caused by Corynebacterium minutissimum (gram-positive rod). Coral-red fluorescence under Wood's lamp is due to coproporphyrin III produced by the bacteria — pathognomonic. KOH is negative (bacterial, not fungal). Diabetes and obesity are risk factors. Treatment: topical erythromycin or oral erythromycin 250mg QID for 2 weeks.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman presents with yellowish-white, thickened, brittle, crumbly nails affecting both great toenails. There is subungual hyperkeratosis and onycholysis. The most common dermatophyte responsible for distal subungual onychomycosis of toenails is:
questions.exp: Trichophyton rubrum accounts for approximately 70-90% of all cases of onychomycosis worldwide, especially toenail DLSO (distal lateral subungual onychomycosis). Gold standard treatment: oral terbinafine 250mg daily (6 weeks for fingernails, 12-16 weeks for toenails). Nail clipping PAS stain is diagnostic.

questions.q: A 25-year-old sexually active woman presents with multiple soft, moist, cauliflower-like exophytic growths over the vulva and perianal region. They are painless and non-pruritic. The HPV types most responsible for these anogenital warts are:
questions.exp: Condyloma acuminata (genital warts) are caused by low-risk HPV types 6 and 11, which have low malignant potential. High-risk HPV 16 and 18 are responsible for cervical, vulvar, penile, and oropharyngeal carcinomas. Gardasil-9 vaccine covers HPV 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, 58.

questions.q: A 7-year-old girl presents with pruritic clustered vesicles and tense bullae in a 'cluster of jewels' annular arrangement over the perineum and inner thighs. DIF shows linear IgA deposits at the dermoepidermal junction. Which drug is the most common adult trigger of a clinically similar drug-induced condition?
questions.exp: Chronic bullous disease of childhood (pediatric linear IgA disease) shows the characteristic 'cluster of jewels' arrangement. In adults, linear IgA bullous dermatosis (LABD) can be drug-induced — vancomycin is the most common culprit. DIF shows linear IgA at BMZ (lamina lucida). Treatment: dapsone.

questions.q: A 60-year-old diabetic man presents with 3 days of severe burning pain followed by grouped vesicles on erythematous base along the right T4 dermatome, not crossing the midline. To prevent post-herpetic neuralgia, antiviral therapy must be initiated:
opts: At any time during active vesiculation
questions.exp: Antivirals (valacyclovir 1g TID, famciclovir 500mg TID, or acyclovir 800mg 5×/day for 7 days) reduce severity and duration of herpes zoster and decrease risk of post-herpetic neuralgia if started within 72 hours of rash onset. Older age, severe pain at onset, and extensive rash are risk factors for PHN.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman presents with malar butterfly rash triggered by sunlight, bilateral non-scarring alopecia, and recurrent painful oral ulcers. ANA is positive at 1:640, speckled pattern. Which antibody has the highest specificity for systemic lupus erythematosus?
questions.exp: Anti-Sm (Smith antigen — snRNP proteins) has ~99% specificity for SLE, making it the most specific antibody, though sensitivity is only 25-30%. Anti-dsDNA is also highly specific (~95%) and correlates with disease activity and lupus nephritis. Anti-Ro causes neonatal lupus and SCLE. Anti-centromere is seen in CREST syndrome.

questions.q: Melanocytes are the pigment-producing cells of the skin. They are derived from which embryonic structure, and where do they predominantly reside in adult skin?
opts: Neural crest cells; stratum basale (basal layer)
questions.exp: Melanocytes originate from neural crest cells during embryogenesis and migrate to the epidermis, uveal tract, hair follicles, and leptomeninges. In adult skin, they reside in the stratum basale at a ratio of approximately 1 melanocyte per 4-10 basal keratinocytes. Melanin is transferred via melanosomes through dendritic processes to surrounding keratinocytes.

questions.q: A 70-year-old farmer with chronic solar damage develops a firm, indurated, ulcerated nodule with raised, everted edges on his lower lip. Biopsy confirms well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma. The most common precursor lesion for SCC on the lip is:
questions.exp: Actinic cheilitis is the most common precursor of SCC of the lower lip. The lower lip receives more direct UV radiation than the upper lip. Malignant transformation rate of actinic cheilitis is 10-20%. Lower lip SCC has significant metastatic potential (~10-15%). Erythroplakia has the highest overall malignant transformation rate among oral premalignant lesions.

questions.q: A dermatologist performs a Tzanck smear from the base of a fresh blister in a patient with grouped vesicles on erythematous skin. The smear reveals large multinucleated giant cells with nuclear molding and a 'steel-gray' appearance of nuclear membranes. This finding is diagnostic of:
questions.exp: Multinucleated giant cells (Tzanck cells) with nuclear molding and margination of chromatin are diagnostic of herpes virus infections (HSV-1, HSV-2, VZV). Pemphigus shows acantholytic cells (rounded keratinocytes with large nuclei) but not multinucleated giant cells. Tzanck smear cannot distinguish between HSV and VZV; PCR or DIF is required.

questions.q: A 40-year-old man on methotrexate for severe psoriasis develops fatigue and a macrocytic anemia at 6 months. To minimize hematologic side effects while maintaining anti-inflammatory efficacy, the best approach is:
opts: Add folic acid 5mg daily on days when methotrexate is NOT taken
Add folinic acid (leucovorin) on the same day as methotrexate
questions.exp: Folic acid 5mg daily (on non-MTX days) reduces GI side effects, mouth ulcers, and hematologic toxicity without significantly diminishing anti-psoriatic efficacy. Folinic acid (leucovorin) is reserved for acute MTX toxicity rescue. Supplementation should be started alongside methotrexate prophylactically. LFTs and CBC monitored regularly.

questions.q: A patient with lepromatous leprosy on MDT suddenly develops acute high fever, multiple tender erythematous nodules over limbs, arthritis, iritis, and orchitis. The drug of choice for this severe type 2 lepra reaction is:
questions.exp: Erythema nodosum leprosum (ENL) is a Type 2 reaction in lepromatous (LL) and borderline lepromatous (BL) leprosy caused by immune complex deposition. Thalidomide (200-400 mg/day) is the drug of choice due to potent anti-TNF-alpha action. Absolutely contraindicated in women of childbearing potential (severe teratogenicity). Prednisolone is used when thalidomide is contraindicated.

questions.q: A 55-year-old agricultural worker from Kerala presents with a 12-year-old verrucous, warty, hyperkeratotic, cauliflower-like plaque on the lower leg. Biopsy shows 'Medlar bodies' (copper-penny sclerotic cells) within giant cells. The treatment of choice is:
opts: Itraconazole 200mg BD with or without terbinafine
questions.exp: Chromoblastomycosis is caused by dematiaceous (black) fungi — Fonsecaea pedrosoi is most common in India. Medlar (sclerotic/copper-penny) bodies in tissue are pathognomonic. Itraconazole 200mg BD for 12-24 months is the gold standard; combining with terbinafine 250mg daily improves outcomes for refractory cases. Small lesions can be excised with antifungal coverage.

questions.q: A 19-year-old girl presents with depigmented patches over the dorsal hands, lips, and perioral area. Wood's lamp shows chalk-white fluorescence. She has autoimmune hypothyroidism. The first-line treatment for localized non-facial vitiligo in this young patient is:
opts: Oral minipulse betamethasone (5mg on 2 consecutive days/week)
questions.exp: Topical corticosteroids (TCS) are first-line for localized vitiligo involving non-facial, non-flexural areas. Tacrolimus/pimecrolimus are preferred for face and flexures to avoid skin atrophy and telangiectasia. NB-UVB is first-line for widespread vitiligo (>20% BSA). Oral minipulse steroids are used for rapidly spreading/unstable vitiligo.

questions.q: A 28-year-old man presents with a circular 5cm patch of complete hair loss on the scalp. The patch is smooth with no scarring or inflammation. Exclamation mark hairs are noted at the periphery. He also has nail pitting. Dermoscopy shows yellow dots and black dots. What is the diagnosis, and what do 'exclamation mark hairs' signify?
opts: Alopecia areata — tapered, broken hairs at the margin of active patch
questions.exp: Alopecia areata is non-scarring alopecia with exclamation mark hairs (hair shafts that taper proximally toward the scalp, resembling '!') at the active expanding margin. Yellow dots (follicular keratinous plugs) and black dots (cadaverized hair fragments) are dermoscopic features. Nail pitting is the most common associated finding.

questions.q: A 70-year-old man presents with tense, fluid-filled blisters arising on urticarial plaques over the trunk and flexures. Oral mucosa is spared. Nikolsky's sign is negative. DIF shows linear IgG and C3 at the basement membrane zone. The target autoantigens in this condition are:
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid (most common autoimmune blistering disease in elderly) targets hemidesmosomal proteins: BP180 (collagen XVII, NC16A domain — pathogenic IgG) and BP230 (BPAG1). Tense blisters (vs flaccid in pemphigus), negative Nikolsky's sign, linear IgG/C3 at BMZ on DIF. Treatment: potent topical steroids or systemic steroids.

questions.q: A 35-year-old man presents with painless, beefy-red, progressive ulceration of the glans penis described as 'beefsteak appearance'. There is no regional lymphadenopathy. Tissue smear from the lesion shows 'Donovan bodies' — bipolar-staining coccobacilli within the cytoplasm of large mononuclear cells giving a 'closed safety pin' appearance. The causative organism is:
questions.exp: Donovanosis (granuloma inguinale) caused by Klebsiella granulomatis (formerly Calymmatobacterium granulomatis). Classic: painless, progressive, beefy-red ulcer without lymphadenopathy. Donovan bodies (intracytoplasmic, bipolar-staining organisms in macrophages) are pathognomonic. Treatment: doxycycline 100mg BD for minimum 3 weeks until complete healing.

questions.q: Langerhans cells are the primary antigen-presenting cells (APCs) of the epidermis. What is their pathognomonic ultrastructural organelle on electron microscopy, and which cell surface marker identifies them immunohistochemically?
questions.exp: Langerhans cells contain Birbeck granules (rod-shaped or tennis-racket-shaped organelles) — their ultrastructural hallmark on EM. Immunohistochemically, they express CD1a, S-100 protein, and Langerin (CD207). They originate from bone marrow precursors, comprise 2-8% of epidermal cells, and are pathologically increased in Langerhans cell histiocytosis (Letterer-Siwe, Hand-Schüller-Christian, eosinophilic granuloma).

questions.q: A 55-year-old man presents with a 15-year history of pruritic, scaly erythematous plaques distributed over sun-protected areas (buttocks, lower trunk). Biopsy shows epidermotropism of atypical lymphocytes with cerebriform nuclei and Pautrier's microabscesses. T-cell receptor gene rearrangement is clonal. His plaques involve >10% BSA, lymph nodes are not enlarged, and peripheral blood smear is normal. What is his stage?
opts: Stage IB — plaque/patch disease, >10% BSA, no nodal/blood involvement
Stage IIA — skin + clinically abnormal lymph nodes
questions.exp: Mycosis fungoides (most common primary cutaneous T-cell lymphoma) is staged by TNMB criteria. Stage IB = T2 (plaque/patch >10% BSA) + N0 (no lymph nodes) + M0 + B0 (no blood involvement). Pautrier's microabscesses and cerebriform lymphocytes with epidermotropism are classic histological hallmarks. Median survival for IB is 12 years.

questions.q: A 10-year-old child presents with a scaly, broken-hair patch on the scalp. Wood's lamp examination reveals bright green fluorescence of the affected hairs. The most likely causative dermatophyte is:
questions.exp: Wood's lamp (365 nm UV) shows bright blue-green fluorescence in Microsporum canis and Microsporum audouinii tinea capitis due to pteridine production by the fungus. Trichophyton species do NOT fluoresce. Microsporum causes ectothrix infection (spores outside hair shaft). Trichophyton tonsurans (most common in USA) causes endothrix (spores within shaft) — no fluorescence, creates 'black dot' pattern.

questions.q: A 50-year-old woman with limited systemic sclerosis (CREST syndrome) presents with progressive digital tip ulcers, telangiectases, calcinosis cutis, and Raynaud's phenomenon. Her ANA pattern shows centromere staining. Which antibody is most closely associated with limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis?
questions.exp: Anti-centromere antibody (ACA) is present in ~70-80% of limited systemic sclerosis (CREST: Calcinosis, Raynaud's, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia) and is associated with lower risk of pulmonary fibrosis. Anti-Scl-70 is associated with diffuse systemic sclerosis and pulmonary fibrosis. Anti-RNA polymerase III is associated with diffuse SSc and renal crisis.
